newsitem.title: UK: Orangemen pull back from brink, Adams cautious.
newsitem.headline: Orangemen pull back from brink, Adams cautious.

text.p: Northern Ireland's Orange Order called off four potentially violent parades on Friday in a dramatic about-face which rekindled hopes that the IRA would match the concession with a new ceasefire.

Gerry Adams, president of Sinn Fein, the Irish Republican Army's political wing, welcomed the unprecedented scrapping of four of the Protestant order's most cherished processions but refused to speculate on the likelihood of a new truce.
"I am not going to speculate about the IRA. I cannot speculate about how the IRA will respond to these developments," Adams told a Belfast news conference.

The centuries-old Protestant organisation called off four marches after intense political pressure and the threat of mass counter-demonstrations across the province by Roman Catholics who see the annual displays as intimidation on their doorsteps.
However friction continued over two smaller marches in the rural mainly Catholic villages of Dunloy and Bellaghy where anti-parade feeling has been running high for some weeks.
Jeffrey Donaldson, a leader of the Orange Order, accused villagers of failing to match Protestant goodwill.
"I regret that tomorrow once again in these areas Orangemen will be faced with the prospect of confrontation and violence perhaps against their parades," he told BBC radio.
Dunloy residents' spokesman Paddy O'Kane said his village was 100 percent nationalist but an accommodation could be reached if Orangemen held talks.

"(The parade) is not acceptable in a nationalist village and it could be acceptable...provided that the Loyal Orders within the village sit down and talk to us. We can work out an agreement," O'Kane said.
In the town of Newtownbutler, Catholics and Protestants reached a compromise about a Saturday parade.

Adams' Catholic-backed party, which shares the IRA's goal of ending British rule of Northern Ireland, came under pressure from Britain and Ireland to reciprocate the Orange Order's gesture by calling a new truce in the 28-year IRA guerrilla war.
Mo Mowlam, Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, said: "I hope the IRA call a new ceasefire."
Britain and Ireland, backers of slow-moving peace talks between pro-British Protestants and pro-Irish Catholics, say the IRA must restore its broken 17-month truce to join the talks.

Irish Foreign Minister Ray Burke said: "The Republican movement should seize the opportunity to participate with the rest of us in the construction of a political settlement without further delay or equivocation."

The decision to call off the contentious parades, on the eve of the "Glorious 12th of July," which marks King William of Orange's 1690 routing of a Catholic monarch that gave the Order its name, was disputed by right-wing Protestant leaders fearful of a "sell-out" to Catholics.
Ian Paisley, leader of the small Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), said it had been forced on the Orange Order to appease Sinn Fein and the IRA and get them to the talks at any price.
"I'll not be talking to these gunmen, I will not be talking to those that hold on to their murder weapons," he said.
The decision exposed divisions in the order, a bastion of Protestant faith and British loyalty. Joel Patton, leader of a right-wing faction, said, "It isn't a compromise. It's a capitulation."
The Belfast County Lodge or branch deplored the decision not to parade down Belfast's Lower Ormeau Road where militant Catholics had threatened to swamp any parade with mass protest.
The lodge said Britain had bowed to "threats of nationalist violence orchestrated by Sinn Fein/IRA."
It urged Paisley's DUP and the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), the most powerful political group in the province, to walk out of the peace talks in protest.
